# Wrap-Up

<Twemoji tag="span">🌠 🌠 </Twemoji>What a hunt\! Congratulations to all of the
solvers of the Galactic Puzzle Hunt for putting the stars back in the sky and
solving an extremely large number of puzzles\! This year, by the numbers we had:

- **411** puzzles (with 132 written by participants)
- **1,097** teams solving at least one puzzle
- **168,394** total puzzle solves

Special congratulations to the **294** teams that finished the hunt, and to the fastest three teams to finish, who were:

1. <Team teamId="749" />
2. <Team teamId="203" />
3. <Team teamId="771" />

The 2024 Galactic Puzzle Hunt had _far_ more puzzles than usual. We tried to focus on small, bite-sized ideas, ordering them randomly and feeding them to solvers in an addicting and never-ending stream. We’ll discuss the design process and construction of the hunt, our reflections about what worked and what didn’t, and the fun we had with you all during the week of the event.

Spoilers below\!

## By the numbers

Here are some astounding statistics about our "number go up" hunt:

- **357,834,729** dust obtained. We’re sorry? Maybe.
- **399,138** times you all pressed "Wish".
- **386,552** total guesses.
- **110,099** canned hints found.
- **9,402** custom hint requests.
- **6,491** times teams guessed FAIR PLAY, the answer to <Puzzle puzName="puz325" />, whose answer was notably found on the "rules" page.

We’re incredibly proud of having delivered hundreds of thousands of aha moments to thousands of people. More statistics can be found at <RoutedLink path="/wrapup/stats">Appendix: Statistics</RoutedLink>.

## Plot summary

You arrive at the hunt hoping for a relaxing evening of stargazing. But to your dismay, there don’t seem to be any stars\! You wish they would come back… suddenly, a star named Stelle lands right next to you. Stelle tells you that by collecting Hope and making a wish, you’ll get a random gift: a new star, perhaps, or a cool artifact, or some also-cool space dust. By making lots of wishes and solving lots of puzzles, you return the stars to the night sky. There seem to be a lot of “star puzzles” that need restoration—hundreds, in fact.

As you make more wishes, you encounter seven Celestials residing in the cosmos, who for some reason have ceased their job of lighting up the stars. You help solve their problems, giving them new Hope and making the sky steadily brighter. In the end, by solving a final metapuzzle, you are able to reunite the Celestials so that they will once again make the stars twinkle and shine. Thanks to your heroic efforts, the night sky is restored\!

![Certificate](/static/images/wrapup/certificate.png)

## Writing the hunt

### Goals

Our goals for the hunt were:

- Make a hunt that’s fun and creative.
- Give writers opportunities to write a variety of puzzles and contribute to all aspects of hunt-writing, such as web development or art.
- Innovate hunt structure, be a bit transgressive (although we were pretty sure it wouldn’t be quite as dramatic as [last year’s card game](https://2023.galacticpuzzlehunt.com/)).
- Spend time as a community, don’t overscope or overwork, and **don’t burn anyone out.**

### Timeline

- March: Kickoff meeting. Two weeks to brainstorm themes, two weeks to flesh out an initial demo. Theme voting.
- April: Demo Day, where everyone shared demos of puzzles, art, story, little web things, etc. Editing started. We hit 100 micropuzzles.
- May: Final meta written. Celestial answers released. We hit 200 micropuzzles. Website MVP.
- June: Retreat. Gacha (hope, wishing, and hint release) mechanics drafted. Celestial answers assigned. Hunt postponed (from July to September). Hunt announced.
- July: Website structure fully implemented. Half of the cutscenes written. Medium Big TestSolve (BTS). Micropuzzle submissions ended. All Celestials written. Half of the micropuzzles postprodded.
- August: All Celestials tested. All puzzles postprodded. Big BTS. UI revamp and star map. Initial art assets.
- September: Final meta revised and retested. Website issues closed. All puzzles factchecked. Hunt started.

### Theme

The original theme proposal was titled “1000 Puzzles”. It was inspired by a mini-hunt written by Patrick, who had challenged himself to write one puzzle each day in the month of November. The theme proposed a huge number of small puzzles which we internally referred to as “micropuzzles”.

After we selected the theme, several mechanisms were proposed to unify the puzzles together, and a "gacha" mechanism was most popular. The plot to “restore the stars” by making wishes was suggested in a second round of voting after Demo Day. We also decided around that time to include the Celestials, who would be characters associated with a smaller number of larger and more difficult puzzles, the “macropuzzles”.

The similarities to Genshin Impact were unintended at first. Later in development, we leaned into it, and it helped inspire some of the art and dialogue. Any references to Honkai Star Rail are completely unintentional.

### Writing

To reduce friction in submission and testsolving, we used a Discord forum with one thread per micropuzzle, allowing decentralized submission, solving, and discussion and editing via tags and emoji reactions. Team members would testsolve puzzles by guessing in spoiler tags, and the author would react to guesses with <Twemoji tag="span">✅</Twemoji> or <Twemoji tag="span">❌</Twemoji>. Editing discussions occurred in the same thread.

To encourage volume of puzzles, there were almost no constraints on puzzle format, topic, or answer. Puzzles quickly became unhinged, ranging from stupid jokes to identification tasks to things which barely resemble puzzles at all.

While puzzles were originally intended to be independent, sequences of puzzles arose organically as puzzle authors were inspired by other existing puzzles (<Puzzle puzName="puz49" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz40" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz126" />). Other authors then chose to write small sequences with metas (<Puzzle puzName="puz67" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz212" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz72" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz285" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz105" />).

After receiving two clean testsolves, each puzzle needed approval from two editors, a postprodded version on the website, and a factcheck. Puzzle progress was tracked on the forum, with the help of a Discord bot that output statuses onto a Google Sheet.

### Operations

We redid the hint queue from past years into a general “admin queue” that held tasks for every kind of team interaction. In addition to hint requests, we had tasks for tree-hugging photos, Musical Intuition submissions, and Free Puzzle submissions. Teams could submit custom puzzles as a part of <Puzzle puzName="puz105" />, which we organized and edited in a Discord forum, similar to what we did for micropuzzles. We attempted to get a clean testsolve (ideally two) for each submission, which sometimes took a while especially if your puzzle was difficult\!

## Reflections

### Hunt experience

The central defining structure of this hunt was the "gacha", which enabled solvers to "wish" for any number of things, from dust, to artifacts, to hints, to puzzles, big and more importantly, small. The result was a high-velocity hunt that several solvers compared to scrolling TikTok. Others described it as addicting; in fact, when testing our own website, we ourselves even found the experience of pressing "wish", listening to the notification sound, and watching the animation exhilarating, despite knowing all of the answers to our own puzzles.

While this structure had many desirable properties for solver experience, one of the biggest advantages was organizational. As a team of volunteers, it’s difficult to ensure a commitment to writing a certain number of puzzles year after year. The format allowed us flexibility to write puzzles with fewer constraints and timelines; see <RoutedLink path="/wrapup/fluidity">Appendix: On Fluidity</RoutedLink> for more thoughts.

### Micropuzzles

The focus of the hunt was on the micropuzzle experience. We hoped that micropuzzles were a fun change of pace from the relatively difficult puzzles typically seen in Galactic Puzzle Hunt, while the Celestial puzzles would provide more traditional material for those who wanted to invest more effort into their solves. Setting difficult but approachable puzzles is a constant challenge for puzzle writing, and we hope to take some of the lessons from this year’s hunt into the future.

In the initial stages of planning, we had some reasonable doubts about micropuzzles including:

- Would it be feasible for us to write “1000” puzzles?
- Would each puzzle receive enough editorial attention to be high-quality?
- Would these tiny puzzles be fun?
- Is it possible to solve so many puzzles together in a weekend or a week?

These challenges ended up being mostly surmountable. We well surpassed our initial goal of writing 200 puzzles, and had enough capacity to get them all testsolved, edited, and factchecked. While there did end up being a trade-off with puzzle quality, we were happy with the general quality of the 279 puzzles we ended with. (Amusingly enough, we also had a different theme proposal called “40 Good Puzzles”.)

We cut dozens of puzzles we felt weren’t strong enough. The small, modular nature of micropuzzles meant editors and authors were more comfortable aggressively cutting rather than putting more time into salvaging a so-so idea. On the other hand, it was more difficult than usual to justify dropping puzzles, since there was a lower cost to just putting them in. Few of us had the heart to drop our teammates’ puzzles about overrepresented topics or with overused mechanics. Managing the distribution of these puzzles was an unexpected challenge and one we didn’t quite figure out while creating this hunt.

We had a lot of fun exploring what a micropuzzle could be. The flexibility allowed for a big variety of puzzle types and less friction writing puzzles – since writers could just pick any answer they liked. Initially, there was a “race to the bottom” to make the smallest possible "Planck unit" of a puzzle (<Puzzle puzName="puz43" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz33" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz29" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz117" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz317" />). A separate line of ideas just taught you some fun facts (<Puzzle puzName="puz110" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz190" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz227" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz280" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz220" />). We also had a collection of variety tasks and non-answerables (<Puzzle puzName="puz144" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz136" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz139" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz212" />, <Puzzle puzName="puz207" />). Thanks in large part to the bold tenacity of the web team, a lot of the more unusual ideas made it into the hunt.

Feedback from participants in our big testsolves validated our guesses about the hunt experience. While we didn’t get high-confidence estimates of the total length of the hunt, we were relieved to see that several teams finished the hunt well within the weekend.

The result of the micropuzzle writing process was an incredibly varied and chaotic collection of puzzles, which had bottom-up emergent distributions of difficulty, topic, and pace. We’re very happy with the results and think our approach was a success overall.

### Structure

**Wishing.** Puzzles were unlocked through wishes in a mostly random order; see the <RoutedLink path="/wrapup/gacha">Appendix: Gacha Mechanics</RoutedLink> for details. We thought this feature worked well. 116 distinct teams attained first solves; check if you were one of them in <RoutedLink path="/wrapup/stats">Appendix: Statistics</RoutedLink>! We also hope you enjoyed collecting the 33 different artifacts.

**Canned hints.** Canned hints were an interesting new feature for this year’s Galactic Puzzle Hunt. They were intended to be a regular part of the hunting experience. During development, we felt that a canned hint system would be necessary to support our micropuzzles, particularly due to their tendencies to be minimalistic and single-aha, and hard to progress on without the aha. We hope that this system made teams find it rewarding to not need a canned hint to solve a puzzle (due to effectively not having to use as many wishes to solve that puzzle), as well as still satisfying to solve when using the canned hints.

**Metapuzzles.** We were initially planning to write metapuzzles involving all of the answers to all of the stars, but because of the democratized nature of puzzle-writing, few were willing to take on the looming task of combining the ridiculous set of words and phrases team members selected as answers into a giant spaghetti-meta. In the end, we decided to focus on the celestial puzzles as the "important" puzzles and include metapuzzles for some sequences without forcing metapuzzles on to the remaining stars.

### Custom puzzles

As part of solving <Puzzle puzName="puz105" />, teams could submit a puzzle for potential inclusion in the hunt. Free Puzzle itself originated from a small unrelated social meetup, where a few of us were joking about a “Free Yannick” puzzle. At that time, we were thinking of ways to incorporate structure in the hunt that allowed for flexibility in feeder construction. The thought came to require solvers to submit an ordering instead of an answer, allowing for an arbitrarily large number of feeders while still giving the “capstone” feeling that a meta traditionally provides. We hoped that this would spark some discussion about the role of metas in a hunt and encourage experimentation with different kinds of structure more generally. Later on, we figured that having teams make their own puzzle was thematic to the hunt experience of chaos and a constant stream of new content, and we added the ability for other teams to unlock submitted puzzles mostly as a gimmick.

As it happened, Free Puzzle did end up having a great impact on hunt experience, but not for the reasons listed above. We had imagined that we would reject most puzzles for being some combination of low-effort and unfun, in part because we thought teams would want to solve Free Puzzle as quickly as possible for progression. Instead, teams put much more effort and creativity into their puzzle submission than any of us predicted, and we accepted 132 custom puzzles, more than 5× anyone in our team predicted. This is perhaps in part due to the fact that Free Puzzle is gated on all of its feeders having been unlocked, so most teams only unlocked Free Puzzle close to or after finishing the hunt. We also realized that teams enjoyed seeing their own puzzles in the hunt and sharing them with others, and it felt much better to work with teams to revise their puzzles until we felt happy to accept them, even if it meant a lot more work for us.

Including all of these puzzles during the hunt was incredibly challenging but rewarding. In addition to managing the constant stream of tree, music, and hint content, we had to testsolve and edit dozens of puzzle submissions, and even ended up implementing on-the-fly features for teams’ puzzles while the hunt was live. Our apologies if you had to wait a long time for a response\! – but ultimately including all these team-submitted puzzles fit exactly into what we wanted our hunt to be: a chaotic, democratic, never-ending stream of surprises.

### Web

This hunt’s web infrastructure is based on GPH2023’s fork, which adds a Node/React interactivity layer on top of the Django-based gph-site. The new infrastructure significantly improves interactivity and performance by supporting SPA navigation and holding frequently accessed database state in memory. For more details about the interactivity layer, check out [our wrap up from 2023](https://2023.galacticpuzzlehunt.com/wrapup).

Despite the more traditional nature of the puzzles this year, we still made many improvements to our web infrastructure to accommodate the uniquely large number of puzzles and unusual unlocking structure. We felt that interactivity was important this year, even with a more traditional structure; the bite-sized nature of most puzzles meant that teams would interact with the website a lot more often.

Due to the much more manageable size of the database state this year, the Node server generally had a negligible database sync backlog, and redeployment introduced a much shorter downtime. As a result, we were more liberal with full redeployments. The delays faced on Monday night, however, were unplanned. In response, we issued 100 [Apologems](https://www.reddit.com/r/Genshin_Impact/comments/126hgp2/apologems_is_here_and_im_all_for_it/) to all potentially affected teams, which we hope makes up for any inconvenience caused.

We’d like to eventually release the hunt site code publicly, with the caveat that it may not be suitable for many running teams. Operating it requires more technical expertise than classic gph-site, and we’re not confident how well the single-threaded design would fare under Mystery Hunt-level loads. Nevertheless, it might be a good starting point for hunts with medium expected load profiles or high interactivity requirements. We’ll likely continue to use this new infrastructure for future projects, so we don’t expect to maintain or improve classic gph-site as much going forward.
